\framekicker{Learning outcomes}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Session Objectives}
\leadpar{By the end of this session, participants can:}
\begin{isteps}
\item State the \textbf{optimisation vs generalisation} tension, and name the three causes of overfitting: noisy data, ambiguous features, and rare features.
\item Explain the \textbf{manifold hypothesis}, and why generalisation in deep learning is \textit{interpolation} rather than reasoning.
\item Choose an evaluation protocol --- \textbf{hold-out, K-fold, iterated K-fold} --- and avoid the three pitfalls that invalidate it.
\item Set a \textbf{common-sense baseline} before training anything.
\item Diagnose the three training failures: \textbf{won't start, won't generalise, won't overfit} --- and apply the right remedy to each.
\item Apply \textbf{dataset curation, feature engineering, early stopping, capacity reduction, weight regularisation, and dropout}, and know when each fits.
\end{isteps}

\coursesection{01}{Generalisation: the goal}{Why overfitting happens in every problem, without exception.}

\framekicker{Section 5.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The one tension everything else serves}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch05-tension.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont You can only act on one side of this picture.\par}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{The goal of the game is to get good generalisation, of course, but you don't control generalisation; you can only fit the model to its training data. If you do that too well, overfitting kicks in and generalisation suffers.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 5.1}
\end{iquote}
\end{frame}
\note{The key phrase is 'you don't control generalisation'. Every technique in this chapter is indirect --- none of them adjusts it straight.}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The canonical curve --- and it is universal}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/book/figure-5-1.png}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Figure 5.1 --- the same shape appears with every model type and every dataset.~\textcolor{ink3}{\footnotesize---~Chollet \& Watson, \emph{Deep Learning with Python}, 3rd ed. (Manning)}\par}
\begin{ibullets}
\item \textbf{Underfit} --- progress still available; the network has not yet modelled the relevant patterns.
\item \textbf{Robust fit} --- the best point. Narrow, and visible only through validation metrics.
\item \textbf{Overfit} --- the model starts learning patterns \hilite{specific to the training data} that mislead on new data.
\end{ibullets}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Cause 1 --- noisy training data}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Real datasets contain invalid inputs --- an all-black MNIST image, for instance. Worse, they contain perfectly valid inputs that are \textbf{mislabelled}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
A model that goes out of its way to accommodate those outliers gets worse on everything near them: a 4 resembling a mislabelled 4 \hilite{ends up classified as a 9}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Cause 2 --- ambiguous features}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Not all noise comes from mistakes. Perfectly clean, correctly labelled data can still be noisy when the problem itself involves uncertainty.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{No objective boundary.} Is this banana unripe, ripe, or rotten? Different human labellers disagree on the same photograph.\par}\vskip 4pt

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{Genuine randomness.} The same atmospheric pressure reading is sometimes followed by rain and sometimes by clear sky.\par}\vskip 4pt

\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[signal]
A model overfits such data by being \textbf{too confident} in the ambiguous region. A robust fit \hilite{ignores individual points and looks at the bigger picture}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Cause 3 --- rare features and spurious correlations}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}If you had only ever met two orange tabby cats and both were antisocial, you might conclude orange tabbies are antisocial. That is overfitting, in one sentence.\par}\vskip 4pt
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The machine version: the word \textit{cherimoya} appears in exactly one training review, which happens to be negative. A poorly regularised model gives it enormous weight and thereafter \hilite{condemns every text that mentions the fruit}\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[rose]
And it need not be that rare. A word appearing in \textbf{100} samples, positive \textbf{54\%} of the time, may be pure statistical fluke --- and the model will use it anyway. Chollet calls this \textbf{one of the most common sources of overfitting}.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.1 $\cdot$ listing 5.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Proving it: add pure noise, lose accuracy}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Take MNIST and glue on 784 channels of white noise. Then build a second copy with 784 channels of zeros. \textbf{The information content is identical in both.}\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 5.1 --- two comparison sets}{listings/ch05-01.py}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A human classifier would be entirely unaffected by either transformation.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.1 $\cdot$ listing 5.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{\ldots{}and the model is not unaffected}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Train the same architecture on both and compare validation accuracy epoch by epoch.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 5.2 --- same model, two datasets}{listings/ch05-02.py}
\begin{minipage}[t]{1.0\textwidth}
\istat{$-$1 point}{validation accuracy, purely from spurious correlations}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[signal]
One percentage point, from information carrying \textbf{no signal at all}. Add more noise channels and it degrades further. Hence \textbf{feature selection}: score each feature's usefulness --- mutual information with the labels, say --- and \hilite{keep only what clears a threshold}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.2 $\cdot$ listing 5.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{A model will fit absolutely anything}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Shuffle the MNIST labels so that no relationship remains between images and targets, then train for 100 epochs.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 5.4 --- randomly shuffled labels}{listings/ch05-03.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch05-04.txt}
\begin{iband}[amber]
The training loss falls even though \textbf{nothing is learnable}. The model is \hilite{memorising, like a Python dictionary}. So the ability to fit is no evidence that the problem is solvable.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}
\note{The most useful diagnostic in the chapter: training loss falling while validation sits at the baseline means the data does not contain the answer --- it is not a modelling problem.}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{So why does it generalise at all?}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}If a network can memorise noise, why does it ever work on new inputs? Chollet's answer is that the reason has \textbf{little to do with the model} and much to do with the structure of information in the real world.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
MNIST inputs are 28$\times$28 arrays of bytes, so there are \textbf{256$^{7}$$^{8}$$^{4}$} possible inputs --- \hilite{more than there are atoms in the universe}. Almost none of them look like handwriting.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The manifold hypothesis}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{The manifold hypothesis posits that all natural data lies on a low-dimensional manifold within the high-dimensional space where it is encoded.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 5.1.2}
\end{iquote}
\begin{ibullets}
\item A \textbf{manifold} is a lower-dimensional subspace that is locally similar to a linear space --- a smooth curve is a 1D manifold inside a 2D plane.
\item The subspace of valid digits is \textbf{continuous}: perturb a sample slightly and it is still the same digit.
\item Any two digits are joined by a \textbf{smooth path} of intermediate images that all still look like digits.
\item It holds for handwriting, human faces, tree morphology, the human voice, and \hilite{even natural language}.
\end{ibullets}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Interpolation, and what it is not}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{What the model can do}\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{ibullets}
\item Make sense of an unseen point by relating it to nearby points on the manifold.
\item Understand the whole space from a sample of it --- \textit{filling in the blanks}.
\item Chollet calls this \textbf{local generalisation}.
\end{ibullets}

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{What it cannot}\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{ibullets}
\item \textbf{Extreme generalisation}, which humans do constantly.
\item You can spend a week in New York, a week in Shanghai, and a week in Bangalore \hilite{without thousands of lifetimes of rehearsal}.
\item That rests on abstraction, symbolic models, reasoning, and innate priors --- what we call \textbf{reason}, not intuition.
\end{ibullets}

\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[signal]
Interpolation is only \hilite{the tip of the iceberg}. Treating it as the whole of generalisation is a mistake; chapter 19 returns to this.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{And it is not linear interpolation either}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Interpolating \textbf{on the latent manifold} is a different operation from averaging in the encoding space.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[amber]
The pixel-wise average of two MNIST digits \hilite{is usually not a valid digit at all}. Every point on the latent manifold is; the straight line between two points in pixel space is not.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why deep learning is suited to this}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A deep model is a very high-dimensional curve, fitted to data points by gradient descent --- smoothly and incrementally.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{isteps}
\item The curve has enough parameters to fit \textbf{anything}; trained long enough it simply memorises.
\item But the data is \textbf{not} scattered points --- it forms a structured, low-dimensional manifold.
\item Because the fitting happens \hilite{gradually and smoothly}, there is an intermediate moment when the model curve approximates the data's own manifold. That is the robust fit.
\end{isteps}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Two properties that make it work}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardgood}
\cardh{A smooth, continuous mapping}
Required, because the model must be differentiable --- and that smoothness is exactly what helps it approximate a manifold, which has the same property.
\end{icardgood}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardgood}
\cardh{Architecture priors}
Models are structured to mirror the \textit{shape} of the information in their data --- especially image models (ch. 8--12) and sequence models (ch. 13).
\end{icardgood}
\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Training data is paramount}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{The only thing you will find in a deep learning model is what you put into it: the priors encoded in its architecture and the data it was trained on.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 5.1.3}
\end{iquote}
\begin{ibullets}
\item The power to generalise is more a consequence of \textbf{your data's natural structure} than of any property of your model.
\item Curve fitting needs a \textbf{dense sampling} of the input space --- especially near decision boundaries.
\item Sparse sampling $\rightarrow$ the learned curve does not match the latent space, and \hilite{interpolation goes wrong}.
\end{ibullets}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Hence the single most effective move available to you: \textbf{train on more data, or on better data.}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.1.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{When more data is not an option}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The next best thing is to \textbf{limit how much information the model is allowed to store}, or to constrain the smoothness of its curve.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
If a network can only afford to memorise a few patterns, or only very regular ones, optimisation \hilite{forces it towards the most prominent patterns} --- the ones with a better chance of generalising.
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Fighting overfitting this way is called \textbf{regularisation}, and section 5.4.4 covers it in full.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\coursesection{02}{Evaluating machine learning models}{You can only control what you can observe.}

\framekicker{Section 5.2.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why two sets are not enough}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch05-splits.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Tuning on the validation set is itself a form of learning --- and it leaks.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{Hyperparameters} (layer count, layer size) are what you tune; \textbf{parameters} (the weights) are what the model learns. Tuning is a search, and searches can overfit.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.2.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Information leaks, one bit at a time}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Every time you adjust a hyperparameter based on validation performance, some information about the validation data passes into the model.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{ibullets}
\item Do it \textbf{once}, for one parameter: a few bits leak, and the set stays trustworthy.
\item Do it \textbf{many times} --- run, evaluate, adjust, repeat --- and an increasingly significant amount leaks.
\item You end up with a model that does artificially well on validation, \hilite{because that is what you optimised it for}.
\end{ibullets}
\begin{iband}[rose]
Hence the third set. The model must have had \textbf{no access to any information about the test set, even indirectly}. If anything at all was tuned on test performance, your measure of generalisation is already flawed.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.2.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Three evaluation protocols}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch05-protocols.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Pick one. In most cases the first is good enough.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The tell that hold-out has failed you: \textbf{different random shuffles before splitting give very different scores}. That is the signal to move to K-fold.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.2.1 $\cdot$ listing 5.6}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{K-fold, and the line people get wrong}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The mechanics are simple; the one thing that must not slip is the model construction inside the loop.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 5.6 --- K-fold cross-validation}{listings/ch05-05.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Reusing an already-trained model across folds carries knowledge between them and \hilite{invalidates the entire estimate}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.2.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{And then the final model}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}K-fold gives you an \textit{estimate}, not a model to ship. Once you trust the estimate, train once more on everything that is not test data.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{after the folds}{listings/ch05-06.py}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{Iterated K-fold with shuffling} repeats the whole procedure P times with a fresh shuffle each time. It trains P $\times$ K models --- expensive, and the book notes it is especially useful in Kaggle competitions.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.2.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The altimeter on an invisible rocket}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{Training a deep learning model is a bit like pressing a button that launches a rocket in a parallel world. You can't hear it or see it \ldots{} The only feedback you have is your validation metrics --- like an altitude meter on your invisible rocket.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 5.2.2}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Which raises the question the next slide answers: \textbf{what altitude did you start at?}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.2.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Set the baseline before you train anything}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2256\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2068\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.5076\textwidth}}
\thead{Problem} & \thead{Common-sense baseline} & \thead{Why} \\ \midrule
MNIST & \textbf{> 0.10} & A random classifier over 10 balanced classes. \\
IMDB & \textbf{> 0.50} & Two classes, balanced 50:50. \\
Reuters & \textbf{$\approx$ 0.18--0.19} & 46 classes, but very unevenly distributed. \\
Binary, 90:10 split & \textbf{> 0.90} & A classifier that always answers A already scores 0.90. You must beat that. \\
\end{itable}
\begin{iband}[rose]
If you \textbf{cannot beat a trivial solution, your model is worthless}. Either the model is wrong, or --- and this happens --- \hilite{the problem cannot be approached with machine learning at all}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}
\note{This slide saves more budget than any other. Have people write down the baseline for their own case before training anything.}

\framekicker{Section 5.2.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Three pitfalls that invalidate an evaluation}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardwarn}
\cardh{1 $\cdot$ Data representativeness}
Samples ordered by class, then the first 80\% taken as training: you train on classes 0--7 and test on 8--9. \textit{A ridiculous mistake, and surprisingly common.} \textbf{Shuffle before splitting.}
\end{icardwarn}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{2 $\cdot$ The arrow of time}
Predicting the future from the past? \textbf{Do not shuffle.} It creates a \hilite{temporal leak}: the model trains on data from the future. All test data must be later than all training data.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{3 $\cdot$ Redundancy}
Duplicate points are common in real data. Shuffle and split, and copies land in both training and validation --- you are testing on your training data. \textbf{The worst thing you can do.}
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.2.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why transactional data hits two of them at once}
\begin{iband}[amber]
Sequences of events are \textbf{temporal}, and the same subject recurs across many rows. Splitting randomly by row \hilite{violates pitfalls 2 and 3 in a single step}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The fix is to split by \textbf{time} and by \textbf{subject}, not by row --- and to state which you did when you report a score.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\coursesection{03}{Improving model fit}{To reach the perfect fit, you must first overfit.}

\framekicker{Section 5.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Diagnose before you treat}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch05-diagnose.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Three questions, asked in order. Each failure has a different remedy.\par}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{To achieve the perfect fit, you must first overfit. Since you don't know in advance where the boundary lies, you must cross it to find it.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 5.3}
\end{iquote}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.3.1 $\cdot$ listing 5.7--5.8}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Failure 1 --- training never starts}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}When the loss is stuck, it is always a gradient-descent configuration problem. Here is the same MNIST model at an absurd learning rate, and at a sane one.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\icode{python}{listing 5.7 --- too high}{listings/ch05-07.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch05-08.txt}

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\icode{python}{listing 5.8 --- reasonable}{listings/ch05-09.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch05-10.txt}

\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[signal]
All these parameters interact, so the advice is narrow: \textbf{tune the learning rate and the batch size, and hold the rest constant.} A bigger batch gives \hilite{less noisy, more informative gradients}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Failure 2 --- it trains but does not generalise}
\begin{iband}[rose]
The book calls this \textbf{the worst situation you can find yourself in}: it signals something fundamentally wrong, and \hilite{it is often not easy to tell what}
\end{iband}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{The data may not contain the answer}
Exactly what happened with the shuffled MNIST labels: it trains fine, and validation sits at 10\% forever.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardwarn}
\cardh{The architecture priors may be wrong}
Chapter 13 shows a timeseries problem where a densely connected model cannot beat a trivial baseline and a recurrent one generalises well.
\end{icardwarn}
\end{minipage}%
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Practical advice: \textbf{read up on architecture best practices for your kind of task} --- you are almost certainly not the first to attempt it.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.3.3 $\cdot$ listing 5.9}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Failure 3 --- it cannot be made to overfit}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}If validation loss flattens and never reverses, the model lacks the representational power to model the problem. Here is that failure, deliberately built.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 5.9 --- insufficient capacity}{listings/ch05-11.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch05-12.txt}
\begin{iband}[signal]
You can fit, but you cannot clearly overfit --- even after many passes. \hilite{It should always be possible to overfit}, so this points at capacity.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.3.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Too little, right, and too much}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.188\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2444\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3948\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.1128\textwidth}}
\thead{Model} & \thead{Architecture} & \thead{What happens} & \thead{Figure} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Under-capacity} & \inlinecode{Dense(10, softmax)} alone & Validation loss reaches 0.26 and stops. Fits, but \hilite{cannot clearly overfit}. & 5.14 \\
\textbf{Right capacity} & 2 $\times$ \inlinecode{Dense(128, relu)} & Fits fast, starts overfitting \textbf{after eight epochs}. Exactly the shape you want. & 5.15 \\
\textbf{Over-capacity} & 3 $\times$ \inlinecode{Dense(2048, relu)} & Overfits \textbf{immediately}; training loss near zero very quickly, validation loss noisy. & 5.16 \\
\end{itable}
\begin{iband}[signal]
The workflow: \textbf{start with few layers and parameters, and grow until validation loss stops improving.} There is no formula for the right size --- it is found on the validation set, \hilite{never on the test set}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\coursesection{04}{Improving generalisation}{Five moves, in order of how much they are worth.}

\framekicker{Section 5.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The order to try things in}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch05-regularise.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Left to right, cheapest and most effective first.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Every one of these is downstream of the same idea: make the model's curve smoother, or make interpolation easier.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Dataset curation pays the most, and gets skipped the most}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{Deep learning is curve fitting, not magic.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 5.4.1}
\end{iquote}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{Make sure you have enough data.} You need a dense sampling of the input-cross-output space. Problems that look impossible sometimes become solvable with a larger dataset.
\item \textbf{Minimise labelling errors.} Look at your inputs for anomalies; proofread the labels.
\item \textbf{Clean the data and handle missing values.} Chapter 6 covers how.
\item \textbf{Do feature selection} if you have many features and are unsure which are useful.
\end{isteps}
\begin{iband}[amber]
And know the limit: if the problem is \textbf{overly noisy or fundamentally discrete} --- sorting a list, say --- deep learning \hilite{will not help you}, at any data volume.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Feature engineering: the clock face}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2256\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3384\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.376\textwidth}}
\thead{Level} & \thead{What goes in} & \thead{What it takes to solve} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Raw data} & The pixel grid of a clock & A convolutional network, and considerable compute. \\
\textbf{Better features} & (x, y) coordinates of each hand's tip & A simple machine learning algorithm suffices. \\
\textbf{Better still} & The angle $\theta$ of each hand (polar coordinates) & \hilite{No machine learning at all} --- rounding and a dictionary lookup. \\
\end{itable}
\begin{iband}[signal]
That is the essence of it: \textbf{making a problem easier by expressing it more simply}. Make the latent manifold smoother and better organised. It requires understanding the problem deeply.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Deep learning removed the need --- but not entirely}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Before deep learning this was \textbf{the} most important part of the workflow. MNIST solutions were built from hand-coded features: the number of closed loops in a digit, its height, histograms of pixel values.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardgood}
\cardh{Still worth it --- reason 1}
Good features solve problems \textbf{with fewer resources}. Using a ConvNet to read a clock face would be absurd.
\end{icardgood}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardgood}
\cardh{Still worth it --- reason 2}
Good features solve problems \textbf{with far less data}. A model's ability to find its own features depends on having a lot of it.
\end{icardgood}
\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Early stopping}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Deep models are always \textbf{vastly overparameterised} --- far more degrees of freedom than the minimum needed. That is not a problem, because \hilite{you never fit one all the way}\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{The chapter-4 way} --- train longer than needed to find the best epoch, then train a fresh model for exactly that many.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[amber]
Standard, but it means \hilite{doing the work twice}
\end{iband}

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{The better way} --- save the model at the end of each epoch and keep the best. In Keras this is the \inlinecode{EarlyStopping} callback, which halts as soon as validation stops improving \textbf{while remembering the best state}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
Callbacks are covered in \textbf{chapter 7}.
\end{iband}

\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.4 $\cdot$ listing 5.10--5.12}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Regularisation 1 --- make the model smaller}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}With limited memorisation capacity the model is \hilite{forced to learn compressed representations that have predictive power} --- precisely the kind we want.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.1692\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.188\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.1692\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.4136\textwidth}}
\thead{Version} & \thead{Hidden layers} & \thead{Starts overfitting} & \thead{Behaviour} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Reference} & 2 $\times$ \inlinecode{Dense(16)} & epoch 4 & The comparison point. \\
\textbf{Smaller} & 2 $\times$ \inlinecode{Dense(4)} & epoch 6 & Overfits later, and \textbf{degrades more slowly} once it does. \\
\textbf{Much larger} & 2 $\times$ \inlinecode{Dense(512)} & epoch 1 & Overfits almost immediately and far more severely; validation loss noisier, training loss near zero fast. \\
\end{itable}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.4 $\cdot$ listing 5.13}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Regularisation 2 --- constrain the weights}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Occam's razor applied to weights: given the same data and architecture many weight settings explain it, and \textbf{simpler ones are less likely to overfit}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 5.13--5.14 --- weight regularisers}{listings/ch05-13.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
\inlinecode{l2(0.002)} adds \inlinecode{0.002 * weight ** 2} per coefficient to the loss. The penalty applies \textbf{only during training}, so \hilite{training loss will read much higher than test loss} --- expected, not a bug.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{L1 or L2, and when weight regularisation stops helping}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.1316\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.4136\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3948\textwidth}}
\thead{Kind} & \thead{Penalty added to the loss} & \thead{Effect} \\ \midrule
\textbf{L1} & Proportional to the \textbf{absolute value} of the weights. & Pushes weights towards \textbf{sparsity} --- many exactly zero. \\
\textbf{L2} & Proportional to the \textbf{square} of the weights. & Pushes all weights small. Also called \textbf{weight decay} --- different name, identical mathematics. \\
\end{itable}
\begin{iband}[amber]
Weight regularisation is \textbf{typically used on smaller models}. Large models are so overparameterised that constraining weight values \hilite{has little effect on capacity}. For those, dropout is preferred.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.4 $\cdot$ listing 5.15}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Regularisation 3 --- dropout}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch05-dropout.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Figure 5.21 --- the rescaling is done during training so that test time needs no adjustment at all.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The \textbf{dropout rate} is the fraction zeroed out, usually between \textbf{0.2 and 0.5}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{\ldots{}and how it looks in a model}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A \inlinecode{Dropout} layer is inserted after the layer whose output it should perturb.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 5.15 --- dropout on the IMDB model}{listings/ch05-14.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
On the IMDB model this is a clear improvement over the reference --- and it reaches a \textbf{lower minimum validation loss than L2 did}.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Where dropout came from}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{I went to my bank. The tellers kept changing and I asked one of them why. He said he didn't know but they got moved around a lot. I figured it must be because it would require cooperation between employees to successfully defraud the bank. This made me realize that randomly removing a different subset of neurons on each example would prevent conspiracies and thus reduce overfitting.}\quotecite{Geoff Hinton, quoted in Chollet \& Watson, section 5.4.4}
\end{iquote}
\begin{iband}[signal]
The mechanism in one line: injecting noise into a layer's outputs \hilite{breaks up accidental patterns} --- Hinton's \textit{conspiracies} --- that the model would otherwise start memorising.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 5.4.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Which technique, when}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2256\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3196\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3948\textwidth}}
\thead{Technique} & \thead{Best suited to} & \thead{Notes} \\ \midrule
\textbf{More / better data} & Always, where possible. & The largest return. Adding overly noisy data harms instead. \\
\textbf{Better features} & Small data; well-understood problems. & Can remove the need for a large model entirely. \\
\textbf{Reduce capacity} & Small models; small datasets. & Find the compromise --- do not tip into underfitting. \\
\textbf{L1 / L2} & \textbf{Smaller} deep learning models. & On very large models, constraining weights \hilite{does little} \\
\textbf{Dropout} & \textbf{Large} models, where weight decay is weak. & Rates of 0.2--0.5. Beat L2 on the IMDB benchmark. \\
\end{itable}
\begin{iband}[rose]
One condition governs all of them: \textbf{regularisation must be guided by an accurate evaluation procedure}. You will only achieve generalisation \hilite{if you can measure it}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Summary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What has to survive this chapter}
\begin{isteps}
\item The purpose of a model is to \textbf{generalise} --- to be accurate on inputs it has never seen. Harder than it sounds.
\item Deep networks generalise by \textbf{interpolating} on the data's latent manifold, which is why they only make sense of inputs \hilite{close to what they have seen}.
\item The fundamental problem is the \textbf{optimisation vs generalisation tension}. Every best practice in the book manages it.
\item \textbf{Measure before you improve.} Hold-out, K-fold, iterated K-fold --- and always keep a completely untouched test set.
\item \textbf{Set a common-sense baseline first.} If you cannot beat it, the problem may not be a machine learning problem.
\end{isteps}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Summary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{\ldots{}and the two orders worth memorising}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Both are sequences, not menus. Working through them in order is what keeps you from tuning something that was never the bottleneck.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{To make it fit}
\textbf{Learning rate and batch size $\rightarrow$ architecture priors $\rightarrow$ capacity}, until the model can overfit.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{To make it generalise}
\textbf{Better data $\rightarrow$ better features $\rightarrow$ early stopping $\rightarrow$ less capacity $\rightarrow$ L1/L2 $\rightarrow$ dropout.}
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\vskip 4pt
